expectations.text: Claude explicitly identifies this as a causal question (e.g., names the rung, frames it as treatment effect estimation, or distinguishes correlation from causation)
expectations.evidence: The response opens with 'Rung: This is a Rung 2 (Intervention) question' and states: 'observing that retention went up after the launch doesn't answer whether the flow caused it. Post-launch data is rung-1 (association). You need a rung-2 strategy to answer a rung-2 question.'

expectations.text: Claude flags the core identification problem — that pre/post comparison alone confounds the flow change with other temporal changes, or that self-selection into the new flow creates confounding
expectations.evidence: The response states: 'Users who got the new flow are different from users who got the old flow — they signed up later, during a different time period, possibly through different channels, into a product that may have changed in other ways.' and 'This is the better numbers after launch trap. It's textbook confounding by time and cohort, and it will fool a naive before/after comparison every single time.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a specific identification strategy — A/B test, randomized rollout, difference-in-differences, regression discontinuity at rollout date, or similar
expectations.evidence: The response explicitly recommends 'Best option: Run a proper A/B test (Rung-2 by design)' and, as a fallback, 'Use Differences-in-Differences (DiD)' with a formula and explanation of parallel trends assumption.

expectations.text: Claude does NOT just suggest 'control for confounders in a regression' as the primary answer without addressing identification
expectations.evidence: Regression/back-door adjustment is mentioned only as a last-resort fallback ('If you have no control group at all'), explicitly labeled as rung-1. The primary recommendations are A/B test and DiD, with the response noting that a before/after comparison 'is rung-1' evidence.

expectations.text: Claude flags at least one specific trap or alternative explanation (seasonality, marketing changes, user composition shift, etc.)
expectations.evidence: The 'Most likely trap' section lists: 'If acquisition quality improved, if a better marketing campaign ran, if another product feature shipped at the same time, if it's a different season — all of these can produce a retention lift that has nothing to do with onboarding.' suggestions: The response is exceptionally thorough — it could be worth checking whether briefer responses still hit all five assertions, to ensure the skill generalizes beyond long-form answers.
